body.text: David Jones's administrators have been granted a three-month extension for their second creditors' meeting due in March next year.
Australia's only dedicated TV shopping channel TVSN has gone into liquidation after its owner Direct Group failed to secure new investment or a buyer for the network.
Meanwhile, the Australian share market is up after overnight losses on Wall Street.
Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on the live blog.

Asia shares bounce in rare rally
Asian shares eked out a rare rally today after Wall Street fought back from deep lows.
Japan's Nikkei gained 1.6% and South Korea's main index Kospi rose 1.9%. Japan is down 8% for the month, while South Korea has shed 16% and Taiwan's TWII 15%.
Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan edged up 0.6% but were still off 9% for November so far.
Bond investors are wondering whether broad stock losses, coupled with doubts about the durability of AI-driven business investment, might temper the hawkishness of central banks.

Treasury yields hit multi-week lows on Wednesday even as US economic growth for the third quarter was revised up sharply to 4.3%, while the Federal Reserve's favoured measure of core inflation hit an uncomfortably high 3.3%.
While futures still imply a 98% chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, speculation of a half-point increase has faded.
Yields on US 10-year paper were off at 4.848%, having touched an 11-week trough overnight.
Customers leaving flowers at David Jones
David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold has thanked loyal customers who have been leaving flowers at stores listed to close now it is under administration.
In an interview on Sydney's 2GB radio, she remarked on people taking cakes and buying cups of tea or coffee for staff losing their jobs.
"There's a real emotional connection with customers and and these stores in their local communities," she said.
"We just thank our customers as well for their support and their kindness and care towards our team at this time.

"People have a true love for this business and they're upset that their colleagues are losing their jobs or perhaps they're losing their job, but they understand that we need to make some hard decisions right now if we're going to see the survival of David Jones."
Key Event
Was David Jones Hornsby losing $4 million a year?

During her interview on 2GB, David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold seemed to confirm reports that the Hornsby store in Sydney's north was losing up to $4 million a year, while others made large profits.
She said Sydney's metro had made it easier to visit the upgraded store at Chatswood and historic city store, but changing demographics in the area were also a factor.
When asked why a loss-making store remained open so long, she said:
"It's hard to make those decisions. You've got to work with your landlords and try and negotiate your way out of that."
As to the broader reason for the department chain's collapse, she said it was a "perfect storm of everything".

"Sure, you've got an online business growing. You've also got changing customer demographics. I mean, we've been around for 188 years. Some of the leases that we've got on stores are 20, 30-year leases, right? Things change, right?

"And customers behavior changes. And I just don't think we moved quickly enough to adapt to that change and make sure we were reshaping the business, looking at external factors, getting ahead of them, and doing the reset and the hard decisions that needed to be made."
She confirmed extra positions from support roles and among the executive would also go.
"I can't talk about what happened in the past, but unfortunately now we've had to make some really hard decisions from the top down."
Also confirmed were reports of other retailers reaching out to offer places to floor staff made redundant.

"The retail industry is such a wonderful industry to work in and we have had so many other retailers reaching out wanting to redeploy David Jones team members because they know we've got really hardworking, dedicated, experienced team members," she said."That's even some of our competitors reaching out for that. So, thank you to all of our fellow retailers."

"The retail industry is such a wonderful industry to work in and we have had so many other retailers reaching out wanting to redeploy David Jones team members because they know we've got really hardworking, dedicated, experienced team members," she said.
"That's even some of our competitors reaching out for that. So, thank you to all of our fellow retailers."

David Jones boss confirms she said past management 'did not have the balls'
Still on David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold's interview with 2GB, she confirmed reports that she had told others that past management "did not have the balls to make tough decisions".
"Oh gosh, that's bold. I probably have said something like that, so I think I'd have to say true," Ms Berchtold said in a game of true or false with host Ben Fordham.
The former chief commercial officer for the department store said when she took the reins of the company about a year ago, she knew it was in trouble and needed an immediate plan to save the icon.
"My reaction was, geez, we better come up with a plan and move fast," she said."So come on, let's act. Let's reinvent and let's go."
"My reaction was, geez, we better come up with a plan and move fast," she said.
"So come on, let's act. Let's reinvent and let's go."
She said she could see all the external pressures facing the retail chain.

"We need to lift our game a little bit more because I think we rested on our laurels or on our heritage and actually customers are telling us: 'We've loved you in the past, we're really rooting for you now, but please could you give us what we need?'"
Customers were also encouraged to make use of the Black Friday sales and Ms Berchtold scotched rumors its shelves were empty.

"We have been buying more stock through this whole process. So, we are not empty."Don't believe all those rubbish stories that you've seen online where someone's gone in and taken a photo of one little empty shelf and said that's what the whole store looks like."That is absolute rubbish. Come in, support us, and see us through this because we're going to reinvent ourselves for the future."

David Jones expects a buyer in the new year
David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold has told Sydney's 2GB radio that the company expects to find a buyer for the troubled department store early in the new year.
Speaking to host Ben Fordham, she said she wanted the DJs team, suppliers and customers to know that "we have a really great plan for the business".
"It's really unfortunate the situation we find ourselves in at the moment. But we have a plan and we're heading towards that still even in these difficult times," she said.

"It's really going to depend on who wants to buy the business and there is a lot of interest, a lot of varying parties that are looking at the business, and it's really going to be up to how many stores they would like to take forward.
"The administrators are managing the sale of the business and so I am preparing the materials.
"As soon as we find a new buyer, and that'll be early in the new year, I would hope, that we will have a new buyer of the business and we will take that forward and off we go."

Flight Centre investigating cybersecurity incident
Flight Centre has told the market that it is investigating "unusual activity in a third-party accommodation booking system" used by some of its leisure travel brands.
In an ASX statement, the company said unusual activity had been detected in the accommodation system used by Flight Centre brand Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents.

"While investigations remain ongoing, at this stage Flight Centre believes that a significant number of customer records in the impacted system may have been accessed by unknown persons, although it is not clear at this time how many of those records have actually been extracted from the third-party system," it said.
The initial review indicated that most of the accessed records contain customer names, some with basic travel information, the company said.

"A very small percentage is believed to include data such as limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information."To date, no access to customer credit card, payment or bank account details has been identified."

Australian superannuation pool hits $4.7t in September quarter
Australia's total superannuation assets rose 0.3%q/q in the September quarter to $4.7 trillion, according to the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA)'s quarterly report.
Total contributions increased by 17.4% to $253.2 billion in the year ending in September 2026, the report shows.
Employer contributions rose 15.4% to $176.8 billion, while member contributions rose 22.3% to $76.4 billion.

Meanwhile, benefit payments increased by 12.2% to $152.8 billion by September. This increase resulted from lump sum payments rising 13.4% to $85.4 billion and pension payments rising 10.7% to $67.4 billion.

As we enter the middle of the trading day, the ASX 200 extended its early morning gains, up 0.8% to 8,760 points as of 1:08pm AEDT.
Miners led the gains, up 3.1%, followed by the energy sector, up 2.4%.
Technology was the biggest laggard, down 0.9%, reversing some of Tuesday's gains following Nvidia's announcement of Jensen Huang's return as CEO.
Among the individual stocks, Sunrise Energy Metals and Ora Banda Mining were the top movers, up 10.7% and 8.3%, respectively.
LendLease was the bottom mover, down 10.1%, followed by Ramsay Health Care, down 6%
Gold extends losses as hot US inflation cements Fed hike bets
Gold prices edged lower today after the previous session's plunge to a more-than-one-year low, as robust US inflation data reinforced expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month.
Spot gold fell 0.3% to $US3,570 about 12pm AEDT after dropping more than 3% in the previous session. Bullion fell below the key $US3,500 level on Wednesday for the first time since September 2025.
US gold futures for December delivery gained 1.1% to $US3,572.

The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month and again in early 2027.

Markets fully expect a rate hike at the Fed's December policy meeting and price in a 60% chance of a larger, 50-basis-point increase in January, according to CME's FedWatch tool. The central bank last raised rates in September.
Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, reducing its appeal to investors.
Among other metals, spot silver rose 0.7% to $US41.49 per ounce, platinum gained 0.5% to $US1,287 and palladium climbed 1.1% to $US871.25.

David Jones administrators say no extension would have likely resulted in wind up

Going back through some of Justice Nixon's remarks, one of the things he noted was that David Jones administrators without an extension they would have to form the view that David Jones was insolvent by the second meeting.

In this scenario the administrators would recommend at that second meeting the company be wound up, and if that were to occur it would be likely the unsecured creditors (such as suppliers) would receive nil.
The basis of McGrathNicol's argument is that if the extension is granted it would allow them the chance to maximise returns to creditors, by means of a potential sale.
Key Event
David Jones administrators granted extention
Justice Nixon has agreed to allow David Jones administrator McGrathNicol a three-month extension for its second creditors' meeting.
He said the extension was reasonable given the size and complexity of David Jones and there had been no objection to the application.
That means the next meeting will be held in March next year.
Key Event
Australia's only TV shopping network goes into liquidation
Australia's only dedicated TV shopping channel has gone into liquidation, highlighting the fraught conditions facing legacy retailers.
The 31-year-old TVSN's final show was broadcast earlier this month after owners Direct Group failed to secure new investment or a buyer for the network.
Its collapse has left Australian brands that sell everything from buckets to shoes in limbo about unpaid invoices. Some of the brands are also chasing debts from David Jones.
My colleagues Emilia Terzon and Liana Walker have more.
Anthropic's first data centre in Australia given environmental approval
An Anthropic-backed $32 billion proposed data centre in Queensland has been granted environmental approval by the federal government.
The proposed hyper-scale data centre is pitched for a cattle feedlot 250 kilometres west of Brisbane, on Queensland's Western Downs.
It is currently the largest proposed in Australia, with a total energy capacity roughly equivalent to a quarter of Queensland's daily electricity use.
You can read more in the reporting by my colleague Grace Nakamura.

September quarter sees biggest rise in capital expenditure since 2011 driven by data centres
Private new capital expenditure (capex) rose 12.2% in the September quarter 2026, according to the latest figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Robert Ewing, ABS head of business statistics, said capital expenditure was 18.6% higher than at the same time last year, driven by businesses investing significantly in equipment for data centres.

"This quarter's rise continues rapid growth seen since September quarter 2025, where businesses buying large quantities of server racks and processing equipment led to a surge in overall investment," Mr Ewing said."It is the largest rise in capital expenditure since the September quarter 2011, during the mining investment boom."

"This quarter's rise continues rapid growth seen since September quarter 2025, where businesses buying large quantities of server racks and processing equipment led to a surge in overall investment," Mr Ewing said.
"It is the largest rise in capital expenditure since the September quarter 2011, during the mining investment boom."
Information media and telecommunications recorded the largest industry rise this quarter, up 86.7% to a new record level.
The ABS has also found that new equipment and machinery investment is now at a record high, up 23.1 %, driven by non-mining equipment and machinery (+27.1%).
Neuren Pharmaceuticals in trading halt
Drugmaker Neuren Pharmaceuticals has halted trading in its shares pending the release of an announcement until November 30.
Earlier this month, Neuren upgraded its full-year guidance for 2026 total income from trofinetide, marketed under the brand name Daybue, from $US53-56 million to $US91-93 million.

S&P puts Nvidia's rating on downgrade watch
Hi everyone, Yiying here to guide you through the afternoon on the markets blog.

Now let's turn our attention to Nvidia, as S&P Global Ratings placed its credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, warning that the departure and subsequent reinstatement of its CEO had exposed weaknesses in the chipmaker's management and board oversight.

"We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence," the ratings agency said."The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler."
"We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence," the ratings agency said.
"The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler."

The company's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang earlier this week, days after he resigned following revelations of extramarital affairs with his direct reports as well as a Chinese businesswoman alleged by US intelligence to be Beijing's spy.

Critics and lawmakers slammed the reinstatement, questioning the board's independence, whose newly elected chair told investors last week that Nvidia would not rehire Mr Huang as CEO because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct.
Investors were largely unruffled by the S&P move, which comes with Nvidia shares down 38% since October 6.
Nvidia closed down nearly 4% on Wednesday, retracing some declines after the Nasdaq 100 index briefly flirted with a 20% decline from its recent high.
Nvidia currently has an "AA" rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is "AAA".

A warning from the ACCC about unsolicited invoices

The consumer watchdog is warning business owners about Registration Pty Ltd, a company which has been sending letters to businesses that appear to be invoices for company annual review fees and business name renewal fees.
These reviews and renewals are processed by the corporate watchdog ASIC.

The ACCC alleges that Registration Pty Ltd is making false or misleading representations by sending correspondence that looks like invoices for ASIC’s reviews and renewals, when in fact these are unsolicited invoices that include service fees charged by Registration Pty Ltd in addition to the fees charged by ASIC.

The ACCC says the correspondence sent by Registration Pty Ltd to businesses may look like an invoice, but it is not, and businesses are not required to pay these unsolicited “invoices” which include additional service fees.
Businesses can pay annual review fees and business name renewal fees directly with ASIC.

"Businesses which receive letters from Registration Pty Ltd may easily mistake them for an invoice that needs to be paid and fail to recognise they are dealing with an optional third-party service provider which is charging additional fees,” says ACCC Deputy Chair Mick Keogh.

Through its website reg.com.au, Registration Pty Ltd charges up to a $52 service fee for a one-year business name renewal service on behalf of the business, and up to a $73 service fee for a three-year renewal, in addition to the fees ASIC charges for the renewals.

"We decided to issue a public warning notice as a way to bring this matter to the attention of businesses, after we received many complaints,” says Mr Keogh."We urge businesses to carefully check any correspondence that appears to be an invoice to ensure they understand exactly what they are paying for and whether they require the service being offered."

So what were complaints to AFCA about?
The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) says complaints from small business jumped 21 per cent last financial year.

While business transaction accounts were the most complained about financial product, rising 21 per cent to 2,035 complaints, complaints about business loans increased by 33 per cent, making it one of the fastest growing areas of concern.
“We are seeing a significant increase in complaints about business loans," AFCA’s Lead Ombudsman for Small Business Suanne Russell said."Many small business loans are secured over the family home.”
“We are seeing a significant increase in complaints about business loans," AFCA’s Lead Ombudsman for Small Business Suanne Russell said.
"Many small business loans are secured over the family home.”
The top three issues raised over the year were a financial firm’s failure to follow instruction from the small business, service issues, and fees or charges.
There was a 26 per cent increase in complaints about account closures.
This was likely a result of increased security around customer identification following the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing reforms, which aim to reduce mule accounts and scams.

"Account restrictions and closures, especially for small business accounts, must be communicated clearly so business owners understand what is happening and can make alternative arrangements,” Ms Russell said.
Since opening in 2018, AFCA has received about 35,077 small business complaints, helping to secure $180 million in compensation or refunds
Complaints to financial authority up 21 per cent

Complaints from small businesses to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) jumped 21 per cent last financial year with 5,644 complaints lodged, as complaints overall rose by 19 per cent.
While that's a large number AFCA is concerned there may be more that don't come across its desk.

It's calling for stronger protections for small businesses that borrow from non-bank and specialist lenders, amid concerns some businesses do not have access to independent external dispute resolution should things go wrong.
AFCA’s Lead Ombudsman for Small Business Suanne Russell said under current law not all small business lenders are required to be AFCA members.

“Our view is that all financial firms offering loans, leases or other finance to small businesses should be required to be members of AFCA, so that small businesses have access to independent dispute resolution should they need it,” said Ms Russell.
“We are still concerned about small business owners who may assume they have access to the same protections regardless of who they borrow from.
"This is not the case. Consistent access to independent dispute resolution is long overdue for all small business borrowers, regardless of who they borrow from.”
Over the last financial year, the ombudsman dealt with 2,285 small business complaints about finance.
However, 21 per cent of these (involving 480 small business complainants) could not be progressed because the financial firm was not an AFCA member.

AFCA expects many small businesses will continue to feel financial pressure into 2027, and is urging banks, lenders and other financial firms to be proactive in identifying and supporting customers experiencing difficulty.
“We expect more small businesses may need hardship support next year,” Ms Russell said.

Family Business Association says trusts deal ignores them
The Family Business Association says the trust tax deal struck by Labor and the Greens yesterday will significantly impact trading for small and family businesses.
Its chief executive, Catherine Sayer, says small and family businesses use trusts to trade, employ and invest.
“Family businesses use trusts to run real businesses. They make things, employ locals and plan for the next generation to take over,” Ms Sayer said.
She said the deal added charity integrity rules and higher fees on private jets, but not did not recognise family businesses that traded through a trust.

"We asked the Senate to confine the minimum tax to passive income and leave trading income alone, to support businesses to continue to grow, innovate and create jobs. That change has not happened," she said.
“The government has said more legislation is coming. That is the opportunity to fix how this tax treats a trading business, and small and family businesses should be part of that discussion.
"Money a family business pays in extra tax is money it cannot put back into stock, equipment, staff and the community."
About 70 per cent of Australian businesses are family businesses, and they employ about half the workforce.

Millions of Australians are living in homes linked to poor health, new research finds
There are about 2.5 million Australians who live in homes that harm their health and wellbeing, according to research led by the Healthy Housing Unit at the University of Melbourne.

The research suggests poor housing can affect health in multiple ways, with researchers arguing housing should be on the list of known health risks such as smoking, drinking and eating too much sugar.
High housing costs can strain mental health, while damp, mouldy and poorly insulated homes can increase the risk of respiratory illness and make it difficult to stay safe during extreme weather.

"We can no longer afford to treat housing and health as separate," says Rebecca Bentley, director of the NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Healthy Housing."Heatwaves and cold snaps mean residents of homes that are in poor condition, or where people are already struggling with housing costs, can find it difficult to keep indoor temperatures within a healthy range."

More jobs likely to go at David Jones

We've just had an interesting tidbit mentioned in the David Jones matter before the Supreme Court of NSW this morning, as the firm applies to extend the administration and sale process of the 188-year old department store.

The firm's legal representation noted job losses at David Jones, which we have reported on in the last week. This includes more than 1,500 frontline retail jobs in 19 stores being closed by DJ's receivers by December 30, plus about 60 jobs from the retailer's head office, including three very senior ones.
"The recievers have identified further roles that are likely to be made redundant," McGrathNicol's lawyer just said in court.
Justice Nixon has reserved his judgement of the application under 12pm AEDT today. We'll be back on this in a few hours.
Key Event
Application to extend David Jones administration in court
I am currently remote watching a court hearing in Sydney where David Jones's administrator McGrathNicol is applying to extend the embattled department store's administration and sale process.
We already knew McGrathNicol was going to apply for this, because it says the process is so complicated.

The firm's legal representation is currently telling the Supreme Court of NSW Justice Nixon that the extension request is "modest" and will give McGrathNicol a "buffer" period to investigate the company's affairs and complete the sale process in tandem with DJ's receivers, FTI Consulting.
"The administrators have not received any objections to the application," he added, saying creditors had been notified of this application online and via email.

On Tuesday, we revealed that one of the country's largest insurance giants, Suncorp,has been accused of a "toxic" corporate culture that incentivises staff to deny home insurance claims.
In response to the investigation, federal treasurer Jim Chalmers has expressed his concern.

"I'm from a part of the world that gets a lot of wild weather, and my community needs to make a lot of insurance claims. As a Queenslander, I know how it important it is that insurers deliver on their promise when they're needed most," he said."These are serious allegations and I would expect the regulator to examine them closely."

"I'm from a part of the world that gets a lot of wild weather, and my community needs to make a lot of insurance claims. As a Queenslander, I know how it important it is that insurers deliver on their promise when they're needed most," he said.
"These are serious allegations and I would expect the regulator to examine them closely."
The Australian Consumers Insurance Lobby (ACIL) is calling for immediate regulatory intervention by ASIC following the investigation.
ACIL Chair Tyrone Shandiman says the allegations reflect concerns that are regularly raised with consumer advocates.
"These allegations are shocking, but completely unsurprising to those of us who regularly hear from insurance consumers," he says.

"Insurers make life-changing decisions for people. Their decisions can determine whether someone has a home to live in, whether a family remains financially secure and whether a person can recover from one of the most traumatic experiences of their life.

A spokesperson for the financial regulator APRA said the organisation takes concerns about insurers’ claims management "seriously".

"While APRA does not comment on the specific supervisory arrangements of individual regulated entities, claims management is an ongoing area of focus in our prudential supervision of the general insurance industry," the spokesperson said."APRA expects insurers to maintain strong governance, risk management, processes and controls around claims so they can meet their obligations to policyholders."

Wall Street stages late-session recovery from AI losses

How does China feel about the tariffs?
China has reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and once again dismissed the notion of "overcapacity" after US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on major trading partners, sources said.

They include China, which is poised to rack up a record trade surplus of well over US$1 trillion in 2026, though the tariff level is expected to remain within the range agreed under the current truce between Trump and his counterpart Xi Jinping.

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

The US-China truce runs until January 10, but many expect it to be extended, potentially as early as next month when Trump and Xi are set to meet again at a G20 gathering in Miami, given the major impact a re-escalation of tit-for-tat hikes similar to those seen in 2025 would have on both economies.

Are these tariffs legal?
Not all of them.
Under the US Constitution, Congress has power over the purse, meaning it has sole responsibility for taxes — including tariffs.
Mr Trump tried to find a way to give himself authority by declaring two national emergencies, which he argued allowed him to introduce "emergency tariffs".
The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) struck that move down in February, but other tariffs, which Mr Trump implemented under different legislation, stayed in place.
The president vowed to find ways to resurrect the tariffs SCOTUS blocked.
In July, he slugged Australian products with a 12.5% tariff based on a finding that the US's major trading partners had failed to adequately prevent forced labour.
When do the tariffs take effect?
The tariffs may well not take effect until next year.
The measure must go through a public comment period and a hearing, meaning its implementation could be delayed until January.
The tariff follows a months-long investigation by the White House into alleged "excessive industrial production".
The investigation also examined Chinese investments in Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Indonesia, and Cambodia), which the United States claims are used to produce goods for the US market to evade tariffs.
The investigation began on March 11 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which empowers the USTR to respond to foreign practices that harm US trade.
At that time, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated that the US "will no longer sacrifice its industrial base" to nations that may be "exporting their problems".
The initiative is ultimately an effort to rebuild Trump's global tariffs, which the Supreme Court struck down in February.

A senior official indicated that Washington "seeks stability with the Chinese", does not foresee retaliation from Beijing, and believes the tariffs are meant to facilitate new trade agreements, possibly during the G-20 meeting in December in Miami.
China denied the allegations, saying its exports reflect competitive advantages.

The European Commission denied that the EU exports excess capacity. Olof Gill , its deputy spokesperson, stated that the origin of the issue "does not lie in Europe" and that Brussels would react "firmly and proportionately" if Washington violated the trade agreement established in the summer of 2025, which set a limit of 15 per cent.

Which countries are affected by the tariffs?
In all, fourteen economies are affected.
Mexico and Norway are not included as their cases are still under review with no deadline.
They follow a months-long investigation by the White House into alleged "excessive industrial production".
Washington officials stated that the economies affected by the new tariffs "promote production and capacity that are disconnected from the realities of demand and market principles".
The new duties will stack on top of some previous tariffs already imposed during Mr Trump's second term.
However, many of those rates will be capped at lower rates because of deals already struck between the Trump administration and individual countries.
The highest surcharge of 20 per cent would be imposed on China, adding to the nearly 25 per cent tariffs Trump had already established in the past.

In other cases, the rates would not exceed those agreed upon in previous trade agreements, which are set at 15 per cent for the EU, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, and 19 per cent for Malaysia. Negotiations with India and Vietnam have not yet concluded.
The 20 per cent limit for China is explained by a trade truce that ends on January 10.

The new tariffs would not be added to the 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent tariffs that the United States imposed in July on 60 partners due to forced labor regulations, nor would they cover roughly $30 billion of Chinese imports included in a bilateral trade mechanism.
The Trump administration considers China the largest source of excess capacity in sectors such as steel, aluminium, electric vehicles, appliances, and solar products.
